entries.note: Covered in an earlier idiom episode; most likely wishes someone bad luck so they get good luck, and the hosts reject the 'being in a cast' explanation.

entries.translation: into the wolf's mouth
entries.note: The Italian equivalent of [[break a leg]], which has a set reply, [[may the wolf die]].

entries.translation: may the wolf die
entries.note: The reply to [[into the wolf's mouth]]; the hosts wonder whether the wolf chokes on you or dies before it can swallow.

entries.translation: break your neck and leg
entries.note: A German good-luck wish that is very close to the English [[break a leg]].

entries.translation: break your arm and leg
entries.note: A Hungarian good-luck wish that closely resembles the English [[break a leg]].

entries.translation: neither fur nor feather
entries.note: Said before a hunt to wish that you catch neither mammal nor bird; the expected reply is 'go to hell'.

entries.term: cost an arm and a leg
entries.note: Losing an arm and a leg would be a very heavy price to pay, so the phrase means something is very expensive.

entries.term: cost the eyes of your head
entries.translation: to cost the eyes in your head
entries.note: The French version of [[cost an arm and a leg]]; Rob points out that you lose both eyes.

entries.translation: to cost a kidney
entries.note: The Spanish version of [[cost an arm and a leg]]; Jess thinks it's the mildest price, since you have two kidneys.
Covered in an earlier episode; the idea may be that rain washed cats and dogs living in roofs out into the street.

entries.translation: it's raining ropes
entries.note: Rob's wife once said it in English; heavy rain looks like dangling strings, a French equivalent of [[raining cats and dogs]].

entries.original: il pleut comme vache qui pisse
entries.translation: it's raining like a pissing cow
entries.note: One of the idioms Rob's wife Elodie recommended; another French equivalent of [[raining cats and dogs]].

entries.translation: it's raining chair legs
entries.note: A Greek equivalent of [[raining cats and dogs]].

entries.translation: axes are falling
entries.note: The Croatian way to describe heavy rain; Rob would rather take his chances with the cats.

entries.translation: it's raining dog poop
entries.note: A Cantonese heavy-rain idiom that Jess compares with the French [[raining like a pissing cow|pissing cow]].

entries.translation: crowbars are falling
entries.note: A Bosnian equivalent of [[raining cats and dogs]].

entries.translation: it's raining frogs and platannas
entries.note: An Afrikaans heavy-rain idiom; a platanna is a type of frog.

entries.translation: it's raining female trolls
entries.note: A Norwegian heavy-rain idiom; Rob finds the Scandinavian versions adorable.

entries.translation: it's snowing kittens
entries.note: A cute Norwegian expression for heavy snowfall.
Said about something that is never going to happen; the hosts look for foreign equivalents.

entries.translation: when hens have teeth
entries.note: A French equivalent of [[when pigs fly]], which the hosts compare with 'as rare as hen's teeth'.

entries.translation: on Saint Glinglin's day
entries.note: It invokes a saint's day that doesn't exist, so it means something will never happen, like 'the 12th of never'.

entries.term: when the crayfish whistles on the mountain
entries.translation: when the crayfish whistles on the mountain
entries.note: A Russian way of saying something will never happen, like [[when pigs fly]].

entries.term: slide in on a shrimp sandwich
entries.translation: slide in on a shrimp sandwich
entries.note: Describes a charmed or privileged life in which success comes easily, like being born with a silver spoon in your mouth.

entries.term: to have shat in the blue cupboard
entries.translation: to have shat in the blue cupboard
entries.note: Means making a bad mistake; blue cupboards were valuable because Berlin blue paint only became available in the 1800s.

entries.translation: to tread in the spinach
entries.note: Similar to putting your foot in it; the hosts don't know why it's spinach and ask viewers to explain.

entries.translation: to step on the same rake
entries.note: Means making the same avoidable mistake twice, like a cartoon character or Sideshow Bob hitting themselves with a rake.

entries.term: thinking about the immortality of the crab
entries.original: pensar en la inmortalidad del cangrejo
entries.translation: thinking about the immortality of the crab
entries.note: Used in Mexico for someone who is daydreaming or mentally far away.

entries.translation: thinking about blue almonds
entries.note: Means daydreaming; Rob suggests blue almonds are pointless, which makes thinking about them especially idle.

entries.translation: blowing balloons
entries.note: A Colombian Spanish expression for daydreaming.

entries.translation: thinking about rooster eggs
entries.note: A Colombian Spanish expression for daydreaming, with a double entendre on rooster testicles.

entries.translation: thinking about pregnant birds
entries.note: A Venezuelan Spanish expression for daydreaming.

entries.term: thinking about the immortality of the maybug
entries.translation: thinking about the immortality of the maybug
entries.note: Used in Czech and Slovak for daydreaming; a variant of [[thinking about the immortality of the crab]].

entries.term: thinking about the immortality of the mosquito
entries.translation: thinking about the immortality of the mosquito
entries.note: The Peruvian Spanish variant of [[thinking about the immortality of the crab]].

entries.term: lie back and think of England
entries.note: A British phrase about letting your mind wander during sex, which implies bad sex; Jess says it isn't used in America.

entries.term: the cat climbed onto the roof
entries.translation: the cat climbed onto the roof
entries.note: Means a person or plan seems doomed; it comes from a joke about a servant told to break bad news gradually.

entries.term: to end up like Zabłocki with his soap
entries.translation: to end up like Zabłocki did with his soap
entries.note: Used when a clever profit scheme loses money; it comes from a tale of a man who smuggled soap underwater and watched it dissolve.

entries.term: not my circus, not my monkeys
entries.translation: not my circus, not my monkeys
entries.note: Used to disclaim responsibility; Jess thinks Polish may have had it first and passed it to English.

entries.translation: four cats
entries.note: Means hardly anyone showed up, roughly like 'one man and his dog'.

entries.translation: library rat
entries.note: The Spanish equivalent of [[bookworm]].
Real book-eating pests such as silverfish, book lice or beetle larvae are called bookworms; 'worm' for vermin needn't mean an actual worm.

entries.term: better a bird in the hand than a hundred flying
entries.original: más vale pájaro en mano que ciento volando
entries.translation: better a bird in the hand than a hundred flying
entries.note: A slight variation on the English [[a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush]].

entries.term: a shrimp that falls asleep gets carried away by the current
entries.translation: a shrimp that falls asleep gets carried away by the current
entries.note: Similar to 'you snooze, you lose'.

entries.translation: to pay the duck
entries.note: Suggested as Brazilian and also found in Spanish; means being stuck with the bill or made the scapegoat. Why a duck remains unexplained.

entries.translation: lead a cat to water
entries.note: The Spanish version of [[you can lead a horse to water]], where you can't even get the animal as far as the water.

entries.term: raise crows and they will peck out your eyes
entries.original: cría cuervos y te sacarán los ojos
entries.translation: raise crows and they will peck out your eyes
entries.note: Jess reads it as bad parenting choices coming back to haunt you, or more generally like 'you reap what you sow'.
The name of the crow that follows Jess on runs, a reference to a witch in Terry Pratchett's Discworld.

entries.term: flies don't enter a closed mouth
entries.original: en boca cerrada no entran moscas
entries.translation: flies don't enter a closed mouth
entries.note: Advice to keep your mouth shut to stay out of trouble.

entries.translation: to mount a chicken
entries.note: Used when someone makes a loud scene; the hosts guess it's because a mounted chicken would make a fuss itself.
Most likely from Ecclesiastes ('a bird of the air may carry your voice'); many European languages also mention a little bird.

entries.translation: my little finger told me
entries.note: The French counterpart of [[a little bird told me]], said while holding up the finger; its origin is harder to work out.

entries.term: a magpie brought it on its tail
entries.translation: a magpie brought it on its tail
entries.note: A Russian counterpart of [[a little bird told me]] that features a magpie instead of a little bird.

entries.term: birds hear words spoken by day and mice hear words spoken by night
entries.translation: birds hear words spoken by day and mice hear words spoken by night
entries.note: Means someone will always overhear: if the birds don't tell you, the mice will.

entries.term: you do not sue the devil when the court is in hell
entries.translation: you do not sue the devil when the court is in hell
entries.note: A Cornish saying about situations where the authority that should solve a problem is itself compromised.
Short for 'speak of the devil and he will appear'; many languages have variants.

entries.term: when you talk of the devil, he's not far away
entries.translation: when you talk of the devil, he's not far away
entries.note: A German version of [[speak of the devil]] that is basically the same as the English.

entries.term: when you speak of the wolf you see his tail
entries.original: quand on parle du loup, on en voit la queue
entries.translation: when you speak of the wolf you see his tail
entries.note: The French version of [[speak of the devil]], which uses a wolf; Rob links it to a lingering ancestral fear of wolves in Europe.

entries.term: mention a wolf and the wolf is there
entries.translation: mention a wolf and the wolf is there
entries.note: A listener-submitted Lithuanian equivalent of [[speak of the devil]].

entries.term: between a dog and a wolf
entries.translation: between a dog and a wolf
entries.note: Means [[twilight]], when the fading light makes it hard to tell a familiar dog from a wolf.
Rob suggests it means 'two lights'; Jess says it's more 'between lights', since [[between]] is related to [[two]].

entries.term: the devil knows more for being old than for being the devil
entries.original: más sabe el diablo por viejo que por diablo
entries.translation: the devil knows more because he is old than because he is the devil
entries.note: Means experience teaches more than talent does.

entries.term: to feel it while wearing clogs
entries.translation: to feel it while wearing clogs
entries.note: Used for something so obvious you could feel it even through wooden shoes; the hosts call it quintessentially Dutch.

entries.term: all the Moomins are not in the valley
entries.translation: all the Moomins are not in the valley
entries.note: Like 'the lights are on but no one's home'; it refers to the Moomins from the Finnish writer's children's books, originally published in Swedish.

entries.term: lift the cat onto the table
entries.translation: to lift the cat onto the table
entries.note: Means raising an awkward subject everyone avoids, like addressing the elephant in the room; almost the inverse of the British [[dead cat]].
A British political term for a shocking distraction, as if a dead cat were put on the table so no one discusses the real issue.

entries.term: Norwegians are born with skis on their feet
entries.original: nordmenn er født med ski på beina
entries.translation: Norsemen are born with skis on their legs
entries.note: A saying Rob finds wonderfully typical of Norwegian culture.

entries.term: out on a trip, never sour
entries.translation: out on a trip, never sour
entries.note: Jess's favourite Norwegian saying, which she compares to 'go outside and touch grass'.

entries.translation: to walk around the porridge
entries.note: Means circling a subject instead of saying what you mean, like [[beat around the bush]].
From hunting: beating bushes to scare birds out rather than going straight for them.

entries.translation: to be parsley in everything
entries.note: Describes someone who inserts themselves into every conversation or problem, just as parsley turns up in every dish.

entries.term: he keeps a hedgehog in his pocket
entries.translation: he keeps a hedgehog in his pocket
entries.note: Describes a stingy person: reaching into a pocket with a hedgehog in it would hurt, so they avoid paying.

entries.term: broken Irish is better than clever English
entries.translation: broken Irish is better than clever English
entries.note: Encourages people to speak Irish even badly; it rhymes in Irish and carries a lot of historical baggage.

entries.translation: hunger is a good sauce
entries.note: Means hunger makes food taste better; Jess feels it carries historical baggage but is meant optimistically.

entries.term: don't scald your lips on another man's porridge
entries.translation: don't scald your lips on another man's porridge
entries.note: Advice to stay out of other people's business and problems.

entries.term: one's head is a green pepper
entries.translation: one's head is a green pepper
entries.note: Describes an empty-headed person, like a green pepper that is hollow except for a few rattling seeds.

entries.translation: goldfish poop
entries.note: Describes someone who trails around after someone else, the way poop dangles behind a goldfish.

entries.term: don't call anything splendid until you've seen Nikko
entries.original: Nikkō o mizu shite kekkō to iu nakare
entries.translation: don't call anything splendid until you've seen Nikko
entries.note: Praises Nikko's shrine complex and puns on 'Nikko' and 'kekko' (splendid); the hosts compare it to Goethe's [[see Naples and die]].

entries.translation: even monkeys fall from trees
entries.note: A reassuring saying that even experts sometimes make mistakes.

entries.term: to have one's tongue in one's pocket
entries.original: avoir la langue dans sa poche
entries.translation: to have one's tongue in one's pocket
entries.note: A Québécois expression for a shy or silent person, gentler than the taunting [[cat's got your tongue]].
Jess finds it somewhat derogatory, a taunt aimed at someone who can't or won't speak.

entries.translation: to hammer nails
entries.note: In Quebec French, used for someone who keeps nodding off to sleep.

entries.translation: fasten your toque
entries.note: In Quebec French, like 'fasten your seat belt'; a toque here is a winter hat, though the word can also mean a chef's hat.

entries.translation: under a frog's ass
entries.note: Describes a bad situation, mood or quality; a frog is already so low that being under it means rock bottom.

entries.term: one is a dog, the other is a hound
entries.translation: one is a dog, the other is a hound
entries.note: Uses two Hungarian words that both mean dog; like 'six of one, half a dozen of the other' for pointless comparisons.
